Messages.Author: Andy Brown
Messages.Body:
I was just wondering how often people actually attempt to withdraw,
and successfully manage to.

Last night at the Cambridge Temple meeting, I was playing with my
pizza delivery deck, and ran out of cards. My Prey and my predator
were both gangrel combat decks, I had two Brujah out with 1 blood each,
and 3 pool.

In my untap phase I declared that I would attempt to withdraw from the
game, and passed play to my prey.

He left me alone and concentrated on his prey.

His prey then concentrated on my predator, and took the only two actions
he had to bleed my predator out. Thus passing play to me, and I
successfully
withdrew. (Gaining that all important 1 VP to ensure I came at least
joint
2nd).

However, this is the first time I have ever attempted to withdraw, and
also successfully managed to.

Is this common? If you attempt to withdraw, does it usually mean you
will?

Comments please.

I think that it rarely happens unless you make some kind of deal with your
predator and/or prey who will let you withdraw. This can happen if for
example predator think you're too tough to oust but that they can handle
your prey. It can also happen when the withdraw is mutual. This happened to
me in the first round of Swedish Championships in August. I was playing a
setite (of course!) corruption deck and had ousted all but my predator. I
had Nerferiti up and 8 other minions, all 5 cap or lower plus a corrupter
Courier. My pool was 30+ and still I suggested we both withdrew. Why?
Because my predator was playing Toerdaor with Francois Villon and I had only
a Mr Winthrop out to block with on Nepata (who had SER) and only one blood
on her. Francois also had a Magnum .44 so I couldn't block him in the long
run since I had almost ran out of Majesties. The major problem was however
that he had Felicia Mostrom out with Atonement and a skillcard on her so she
was a 6 cap! Now she could block all but Nefertiti without tapping and she
had a Magnum too. So I had almost no way to get her. My only chance would be
to try corrupt her with Nefertiti and use my Opium Den to eventuelly stealth
by enough of times. He had quite a few intercept cards in the deck though
(but I suspect he had run out of most). I had already 3 counters on her so
it could have been possible, but risky. I had also only one single
corruption card left (which was in my hand) and only one stealth card left
in library, which would mean I'd have to not get blocked on that very last
Corruption action or I could never take her over. He on the other hand had
only 3 minions and couldn't bleed me for that much since I had 9 minions to
block with and he had no stealth. Sure he had Magnums but almost no
additional strikes and I could always hunt with my minions so they could
take another hit after a block. My pool was extremely high and I had also
Khobar Towers. Neferiti was on 5 blood or so after I had Khobar Towered her
(she was a 11 cap too then having a fortitude skillcard on her) and brought
out a new fresh Neferiti :) I could have done the maneuver again to hold out
from Francois but it would only probably have prolonged the inevitable -
that I'd eventuelly would have had all blood stolen of her and no new one to
bring out after Khobar Towering. I had only 3 crypt cards left; 2 Nefertitis
and an Aabbt.

It was pretty much a stalemate so I suggested a withdraw. I still had
librarycards left but if he agrees on a withdraw I can just discard down
till I have no library left and then make the withdraw. A few more rounds
later I suggested a withdraw agtain and he accepted. Thus I got 3 VP and he
got 1. I think it was a good deal for both.

I've only seen one successful withdraw without the others agreeing to the
withdraw I think. But it was so long ago I don't really remember the details
and I wasn't playing.

Roger

Messages.Author: Frederick Scott
Messages.Body:
Andy Brown wrote:
> However, this is the first time I have ever attempted to withdraw, and
> also successfully managed to.
>
> Is this common? If you attempt to withdraw, does it usually mean you
> will?

Not common. Usually, you will not be able to withdraw without your
predator's agreement and sometimes your prey's or other crosstable
players' agreements as well. And usually, if you want to withdraw it's
a situation where your predator would not want you to withdraw.

It happens. If, for instance, you don't feel you can oust anyone else
and will sooner or later be ousted yourself but your predator for some
reason feels like he's better off with you out of the game quicker than
he can oust you, then he might find a reason to agree. Also, in
tournaments I've seen players negotiate mutual withdrawals where they
all quickly draw and discard through their turns until they run out of
cards and then announce their withdrawals. This will likely happen a lot
less often when the table-win rules kick in.

Also, it's been pointed out in this forum that the withdrawal rules don't
always have to result in an actual withdrawal to affect a game. If a
player can attempt to withdraw and for an opposing player to do something
he'd rather not do (e.g. send a vulnerable vampire to bleed him) to
prevent the withdrawal, that may change the outcome of the game.

Fred

Andy wrote:
>>I was just wondering how often people actually attempt to withdraw,

I'm sure plenty of folks *attempt* to withdraw, but you can really only succeed
if your opponents let you. If you are ous of cards and in not such good shape,
you lose nothing by saying at the start of each turn "I declare my intention to
withdraw from the jyhad!", it just isn't going to happen unless your predator
lets you.

Sure, it is *possible* to withdraw because you have no cards left in your deck
and a hand full of Telepathic Counters to reduce every bleed your predator
throws at you, but in all likelyhood, you are going to lose a pool or a vampire
is going to lose a blood, and it is going to fail.

On the other hand, it can work if you can make a deal with your predator or
prey to let you withdraw--the last (and probably only) time I sucessfully
withdrew (with my Rush deck, none the less), I convinced my prey in a game that
had gotten down to 3 players not to mess with me, I wouldn't mess with him, and
he could concentrate on the third guy at the table. My predator's (his prey)
last vampire got torporized by the Renegade Garou with a Meat Hook my prey was
using, and I was left completely alone for a full turn. Thus, I sucessfully
withdrew--I got my 1 VP and my prey got 4 for killing everyone else. Granted, I
didn't have much to deal with, and my prey let me go mostly out of spite at the
third guy at the table, but it worked out for all of us. Well, except the third
guy.

And in a game at Origins, an entire table sucessfully withdrew apparently--it
was a long miserable game that no one was willing, and Tatu managed to convince
everyone that the best course of action was for everyone to withdraw. So they
all did.

So if you can convince someone to let you withdraw, it works, otherwise you
have mostly no hope.

No it isn't. Collusion is specifically an act of behaving in such a way that
someone is gaining an unfair advantage due to people teaming up for out of game
reasons (I want to get my pal in the finals; you said you'd give me 10 bucks if
I help you kill some guy; we decided at the start of the tournament tomake sure
that the guy from out of town never wins a game; whatever).

A table deciding, in a given game, that they all are better off if they
withdraw from the game, and they cooperating to accomplish this goal in no way
falls under the rubric of "collusion". No one is acting on out of game
considerations, no one is giving anyone an unfair advantage, no one is behaving
in any way that is inappropriate to the game.

Messages.Author: Peter D Bakija

J Bond wrote:
>>Collusion has nothing to do with out of game considerations.>>

Specifically in the context of this game, it does. In the context of
competetive VTES, the term "collusion" specifically refers to that which I
explained in the previous post--working together to provide a given player (or
players) unfair advantage based on out of game considerations.

The defenition of "collusion" that I can find (in a Mirriam-Webster dictionary)
is:

"a secret agreement or cooperation for a fraudulent or deceitful purpose".

>>Collusion is not illegal.>>

It specifically *is* in competetive VTES. Cooperation is not illegal. Making
deals is not illegal. Collusion is.

>>Agreeing to all withdraw is colluding.>>

By the defenition set in this context, it is not. Everyone agreeing to withdraw
from the game is cooperating and making a deal.

You can argue semantics and defenitions all you would like, but in this
particular context (competetive VTES), "collusion" specifically has to do with
out of game considerations and is specifically illegal.

Sweet, another collusion thread.

It is really unfortunate that collusion has been the
term used to describe non-competitive or
outcome-rigging agreements in Jyhad games,
since that particular term requires more than
just that.

In the case of a table agreeing to all withdraw,
of course all the players are making a deal where
they cease playing the game to oust their respective
preys and are attempting to rig the outcome of the
game, but they are presumably doing it openly.

Anyway, collusion requires secrecy, and there's
just none to be had in this example.

I'm not defending the practice, I'm really more
criticizing the decision to base Jyhad rules
violations on the standard of
"Collusion to alter the results of a game."

The problem with this standard bit Magic in
the butt several years ago when a judge allowed
a player to openly bribe his opponent into throwing
a match (the judge was later suspended and the
result voided under the "unsporstmanlike" rubrik).

I doubt the players in the Jyhad example
would be cited for unsportsmanlike conduct.
I'm not even sure that they should be, since
they are maximizing their victory points
(though not their game-wins).

Presumably, but whether secret or open, the result is the same.

>Anyway, collusion requires secrecy, and there's
>just none to be had in this example.

If people want to limit it to secret cooperation, I don't think there's much
that can be done about it except come up with a different term for undesirable
manipulation of the scoring system. But, the result is the same. The players
are cooperating in a way that hurts players at other tables.

More generally, there are ways of playing that unfairly benefit or penalize
other players that are extremely difficult to defend against which aren't
secret and don't require cooperation which will produce similar results as true
collusion. With such a narrow definition of collusion, worrying about whether
people are actually colluding or not doesn't seem worthwhile. Most discussions
about undesirable play behavior become arguments over the definition of
collusion rather than whether there's some way to deal with the behavior or
even if there's some reason to deal with the behavior.

>Again, secret agreement and ill gotten gains. These are the pretty comonly

"Ill-gotten" is circular reasoning - it's wrong because it's wrong. And
secrecy is not a necessary ingredient - players might decide to
co-operate in a game because they are from the same country/city or
because they are relatives or because one offers another a bribe. If
such an out-of-game consideration is public knowledge, that doesn't make
it right.

The problem with a joint agreement to withdraw is not that it's
collusion. It's that it subverts the intent of the scoring system. If
the time limit is approaching and it's clear that the remaining players
are only going to score another 0.5 VP then why wouldn't they _always_
agree to a joint withdrawal and so gain an extra 0.5 VP?

Why do surviving players only get 0.5 VP rather than 1 VP when time runs
out? It's presumably an incentive to play quickly and aggressively. If
players routinely agree a joint withdrawal to avoid this penalty, then
the incentive will cease to work as intended. It's not obvious how you
can stop this though. Maybe surviving players _should_ get 1 VP as
standard so that they don't have go through the motions of a fake
withdrawal and can just keep playing the game properly until time is up.

It doesn't help that the VEKN tournament rules require judges to
announce time-limits and tell players when 5 minutes is left. This
obviously encourages end-of-time tactics such stalling and agreements to
withdraw. I try to use fuzzy time limits when I run a CCG tournament to
discourage clock-watching. Last Saturday, we had a 5-player final which
was going slowly - too much caution and hanging back. I warned the
players at 19:50 that I was going to call time at some point before
21:00 - the game might have gone on all night otherwise. I made a
mental note that I would call time at 20:30 - I usually set an alarm
clock but had forgot to bring it on this occasion. I duly called time
and this caught out one player who had been expecting longer. It served
him right as he had been one of the cautious ones - he could have won
the tie-break if he'd been more prepared to stick his neck out. Next
time, I trust that he will be bolder and the game will be more fun for
everyone in consequence.

Andrew

The problem here is as I've argued before. Far too many people take
upholding deals as law. This is further exacerbated by judges that
foolishly allow players to just quit out, rather than "go through the
motions." Actual physical discarding is what allows someone to draw into the
perfect hand and break the deal, and go for the oust, and get 1.5 VPs
instead of 1.

A far more important critique of the scoring system was seen in practice
at the Invitational: Getting 2-2 on a 4 player table means no one gets a
game win, but 3-2 on a 5 player table does. In theory, you need 3VPs in any
case, and 2-1-1 seems more likely that 2-1-1-1, and 2-2-1 hoses the 5 player
table. While it's not clear cut that one type of table is easier to get a
Game Win on, it IS clear that the two certainly aren't parallel.
It's a discrepancy people have ignored in the past, but the "winner take
all" Game Win scoring means it's going to have to be examined more closely.

obviously keep the actual result of the game secret. In the case in
question, collusion would arise if the parties to an agreed simultaneous
withdrawal didn't actual play it out properly but just pretended that
they did. I can easily see this arising in practise as it would be
silly for everyone to go round the table just discarding and drawing
from their deck. Even if they went through the motions, if they weren't
actaully playing the game properly then I would consider this fraudulent
collusion. Clearly what they are really doing is agreeing an
intentional draw and this is scored differently. They would be
misrepresenting the intentional draw as a genuine result so that they
can improve their score and this is cheating.

Note also that the rules also state "Players must not play toward goals
that conflict with the goal of the game as stated in the V:TES
rulebook". The rulebook says "Your goal is to destroy the influence
held by rival Methusalehs." Conniving to allow rival Methusalehs to
freely withdraw is making a mockery of this goal. Tsk.

If intentional draws are allowed then they should be scored the same as
withdrawals and then this nonsense won't arise. If, on the other hand,
you expect players to always play competitively, then you should take it
seriously and not tolerate play-acting.

Andrew

pretty irrelevant. :-) And before anyone's got a VP, it seems a
bit early to be talking about lost causes.

feasible, but I can't come up with any good way to create it
that has both (a) you being one of the last three players in
the game (ie two VPs are taken already) and (b) you not getting
the most VPs you can.
